utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to each and everyone in and around the courtroom. I would like to convey to all of you the Trial Chamber's best wishes for the new year. Mr. Registrar, would you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Judge Mindua. Counsel, good morning and happy new year to all of you as well. For the Prosecution, Douglas Stringer appearing with Matthew Gillett and OTP analyst, Sandra Ramirez Rodriguez, who has been very instrumental in assisting with the organisation of the documents for this witness as well as Case Manager, Thomas Laugel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. For the Defence Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May the record reflect that we sit pursuant to Rule 15 bis, Judge Hall being absent. Mr. Zivanovic, I see that your client is not in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We -- we filed a waiver for his absence. I hope you got it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It has been filed. Okay. Thank you. Thank you very much. So if that's all, Mr. Gillett, you have a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Yes. The next witness is Dr. Strinovic, GH-105.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Before -- before we go to that, the Trial Chamber has a short oral ruling. On the 10th of December, 2012, the Prosecution filed a motion for leave to amend its Rule 65 ter exhibit list by adding nine documents. The Prosecution indicated that it intends to use four of these documents with Witness Davor Strinovic, who is scheduled to commence his testimony today. The Defence does not object to the addition of these four documents and indicated -- as indicated in its response of 24th December. The Chamber recalls that amendments to the exhibit list may be granted when the interests of justice allow. The Chamber is satisfied that taking into account the specific circumstances of this case and the lack of objection of the Defence good cause has been shown for amending the Prosecution exhibit list to include the documents designated with the following proposed Rule 65 ter numbers: 06365, 06366, 06367, and 06368. The documents are relevant and of sufficient importance to justify addition at this stage of the trial. The Trial Chamber is satisfied that the addition of the documents will not result in undue prejudice to the Defence. The motion is therefore granted in part and the Prosecution may add the documents to its exhibit list. Issues as to the admissibility of the documents will be addressed at such time as the documents are tendered. The Trial Chamber remains seized of the motion in all other respects. Mr. Stringer, in order to plan the upcoming weeks and more in particular the week starting 21st and 28 of January, could we ask you to send to us and to the Defence your witness notification for those weeks by Thursday.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We can do that with no trouble at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The witness may be brought in. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Witness. Thank you for coming to The Hague to assist this Trial Chamber. First of all, do you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I can hear you very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could you please tell us your name and your date of birth and also what your ethnicity is, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Davor Strinovic. I was born on the 8th of March, 1949, and I'm Croat by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Strinovic. You are about to read the solemn declaration by which witnesses commit themselves to tell the truth. I need to point out that the solemn declaration that you are about to make does expose you to the penalty of perjury should you give misleading or untruthful evidence to this Tribunal. Please read the solemn declaration now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated. Yes, Mr. Gillett.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, President. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Could you please state your profession and your current positions.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: I am a specialist in forensic medicine, a professor and head of the institute for forensic medicine and criminology in Zagreb. I am also head of the government commission for the missing persons since 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: How long have you been a forensic pathologist?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: I joined the institute for forensic medicine in 1976 and since 1980 I have been a specialist in forensic medicine.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could you briefly explain what a forensic pathologist does.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the specialisation in forensic medicine implies certain problems, mainly in determining the cause of death; that is to say all those cases that are pronounced violent deaths or suspicious deaths where the cause is not clear are the object of interest of forensic medicine. Postmortem is one of the important parts of our job, but pathologists also do other work, primarily testifying in court, and a professor like I also trains students and educates other professionals such as in the police force, writes papers, scientific work, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And when you refer to postmortem, I understand that you're referring to autopsies. How many autopsies would you yourself have performed through your career?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: That is a question that is difficult to give a precise answer to, because I have been a forensic pathologist for 37 years now, and we do autopsies on a daily basis. It's the largest institute in the Republic of Croatia that performs around 15- to 1.600 autopsies per year. There were years when our staff was smaller, and in those years I did 500 to 600 autopsies myself per year, although that number is smaller now, 200 to 300 per year.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And how frequently do you testify in relation to forensic pathology in domestic proceedings?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: I live in the largest city in Croatia with the largest number of courts and judges, so forensic pathologists such as I appear before courts very often or at least provide expert reports and opinions. It's difficult to put a number on it, but I can say that since I have become a forensic pathologist in 1980, I have been in daily contact with forensic work either testifying before courts or writing expert reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And have you testified before the Tribunal as an expert witness previously?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, I have been before this court already five times in well-known cases that you must be familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. You mentioned that you write papers. Approximately how many publications would you have in relation to this subject?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: If you are asking me about forensic medicine as a subject, as I understand, that would be 55 to 65 papers including books and publications for foreign and domestic journals.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: You mentioned that you're in the commission for missing persons. I understand this is the commission for detained and missing persons in Croatia. Can you tell us when this commission was established?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: The commission for detained and missing persons was established in Croatia towards the end of 1991, December 1991, and has existed since then, changing names several times, but it deals with the same problems as before.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And why was it established? What is its purpose?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: When the war in Croatia began, we realised that one of the greatest problems is the number of missing persons. The number varied over different periods, and it was very high at a certain point, and we wanted to establish a commission that would investigate and try to solve such problems and help primarily the families of the missing persons but also the state to restore some order and establish a precise number of detained and missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: So you mentioned the function at the start of the establishment of the commission. Did its functions change significantly in 1995, and if so, how?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: I can say very briefly, perhaps, just to acquaint the Court with the purpose of that commission, we established the commission in 1991, primarily to collect as much data as possible about missing persons and create lists of missing persons including ante-mortal information or any kind of information about the missing persons. We collected that information over four years when we contacted families through the Red Cross and other organisations to inquire with the closest relatives and collect general data but also particular data that are valuable to us such as the health status or some chronic conditions that could be reflected on the bones, braces, protheses that could help with identification. Especially precious were dental records, so we contacted the dentists of the missing persons, requiring all the papers and documentation they had. And here I must say that due to the war in Croatia, most of that medical documentation was not available. So the key information was the one we received from families, the so-called ante-mortem information that is collected over the years. So once you find the body, you can carry out identification. That's what we did from 1992 when we began our work until 1995, and that was preparation for what would follow later when we find the bodies. And the second prong of our job was to obtain whatever information we could from the opposite side that was involved in the incidents in which these persons went missing. So we asked Yugoslavia and later Serbia for such information, later also Bosnia-Herzegovina, to get as much data that could help us later find individual graves and mass graves and identify these people. That was that period from 1992 through 1995 where we did everything possible to prepare for the next period when we got access to these graves and proceed with exhumations. It was not easy to find these graves that had been hidden before, that were subject to natural changes, weather conditions, that were obscured by the vegetation. Anyway, we proceeded with that work, identifying locations, exhumations, retrieving the bodies and matching the information we had before with the -- with the actual state of the bodies as established through autopsies to permit identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: What was your role particularly in that period from 1995 onwards in relation to the exhumations and identifications of the bodies that you found?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Since I was a member of the commission as of 1991, it was logical, as we had to continue the work on identifying graves and carrying out identifications, it was logical for me to take care of the work related to identification. As the graves were located and bodies were found, teams were formed that first carried out exhumations and then the processing of mortal remains. At the beginning there was a lot of such work in all parts of Croatia that was liberated in full by that time. There were many graves, so all pathologists and specialists of forensic medicine were involved in these exhumations and autopsies. All that needed to be co-ordinated in order to cover every location, every grave. All that needed to be harmonised, and that was done through the government commission for detained and missing persons, whereas the other part of the work involving medical experts that needed to attend exhumations and autopsies was done in agreement with me. I did the co-ordination so that everything could operate without any delay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Did you personally participate in some of the exhumations and autopsies of the victims that were found?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. Throughout that time and to date I have been involved in exhumations and autopsies and identifications. At first I did more fieldwork and performed autopsies either on site or at the institute for forensic medicine in Zagreb, because we had prepared premises for that purpose alone. And all the time since 1995, I have been involved very much both as an organiser and a direct participant.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Were internationals also involved in this process of exhumations and autopsies?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I must say I don't know how the work was divided, but international experts came to Croatia on several occasions sent by international organisations to perform exhumations and post-mortems. There were several teams, international experts who performed this work before turning it over to us to continue with work geared at identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: When the internationals carried out exhumations and post-mortems, were representatives from Croatia and Yugoslavia also involved?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Practically with every exhumation carried out in Croatia, several sides were involved, especially international organisations that led these exhumations and the processing. There was also somebody present from the Serbian side, mainly experts from Serbia or the so-called Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: I'm going to ask some more questions about the technical processes of exhumations, autopsies, identifications. Before we get into that, there's a few terms that arise frequently in the documentation, and I'd ask you to clarify. One of the terms is saponified or saponification. Could you briefly explain what that is.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: After death, changes occur on the human body. In the first day or two the changes are not visible. The body is still fresh, as we say, and that is the optimal time for conducting post-mortems, but with time changes progress on the body. If the body is in a humid environment or in water, or in clay, the body will saponify. The body remains compact, the skin and tissue remain intact so that this saponification, which can take a month or longer, leads to changes, but we can still see things on skin like tattoos and scars. On a saponified corpse we can also see injuries such as from a projectile, a knife, et cetera, because the skin is well preserved. Internally we can see injuries to organs. So generally speaking, saponification helps us in processing mortal remains. We have more elements to establish the cause of death, because we can see things that we cannot see on a skeleton.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And in relation to a skeleton, the term skeletonisation, briefly.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: If after death the body is left outside, exposed to air, skeletonisation can occur very quickly, within months, which means that only the skeleton remains without any tissue. That happens to a body left out in the open. If the body is in the ground, in dry soil, it takes seven to ten years for a body to skeletonise. That means that only the skeleton remains, and along with the skeleton parts of clothing. And it's important to note here that when we have only the skeleton, we can judge only by the bones whether we have enough elements for identification or whether we are able to identify a person only based on changes in the bones. And, of course, the same applies to the cause of death. We can establish the cause of death only based on changes to the bones. These changes could be very specific and could indicate with a high degree of probability the cause of death, but they can also be very unspecific or very broad. So we can only say that it's a violent death in the broad sense a result of injury, but we cannot identify the mechanism, whether it's a blow by an axe or a rapid projectile or a shell with high velocity shrapnel. The changes would be approximately the same, broad injuries and very recognisable ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Moving to the process of identification of remains, you've mentioned the term ante-mortal or ante-mortem information. How can this assist with identifying who the remains are?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to start by saying the following: A classical identification that we are going to describe in a minute was the only type of identification up to sometime in 1998 or perhaps in the year 2000. Before then we did not know much about the DNA. In Croatia, the first time we started using the DNA identification method was around that time, and then it became the first and the foremost type of identification for each and every body. When we're talking about ante-mortal information, that was very important, because in 1995 or 1996 or 1997, the only thing we could rely on was the -- a comparison between ante-mortal information and the mortal remains. Like I've told you before, as of 1991, we started collecting that kind of information, i.e., the information that could provide answers to the questions that were raised during post-mortem and when we compared those, we could arrive at some sort of a more or less probable identification. The ante-mortal information consists of the main information such as sex, height, gender - that's what every ante-mortal protocol should contain - and then we proceed to details such as clothes, footwear, jewellery, any objects that may be related to a missing person that could help with the identification, and then we proceed to the body itself. We can conclude that a person could have suffered from an illness, from some changes on the organs such as bones or, for example, teeth. Teeth are very important for post-mortem identification. If the teeth are present, if they're preserved, which is very often the case then with a high probability of almost a hundred per cent we can confirm the identity of the person. What does that mean? Practically it is very difficult to find two people with two identical dental record. When it comes to normal teeth, they can grow in several ways. The gaps between the teeth are different, the colour of the teeth is different. The various procedures that were done on the teeth like fillings, dentures, and so on and so forth. There is a whole series ever elements. And when you have a very good dental status, i.e., very good ante-mortal information that was provided by a dentist or from a medical history, that information is very valuable and such ante-mortal information can help us with our post-mortem identification and provides us with an almost hundred per cent identification match. This was very valuable to us when we first started doing those post-mortems. So whatever we learned from ante-mortal information is entered and is used in identification and that includes the information on the cause of death, because there are witnesses, there are statements. And when you talk to the families and other people, and we have interviewed thousands of people, a lot of people have information about how people perished, how they died, and that part which is the cause of that and similar thing can help and can be used as one of the identification elements. I have to emphasise that when we're talking about classical identification and when we talk about ante-mortal information, the more pieces of ante-mortal information we have and if we find similar things during post-mortem and if we can compare the two sets of data we can establish the identity of the person. We do not like such identification where just one element will be used to establish a positive match. The more positive matches, the better and the more reliable identification. So ante-mortal information is very important, and it was particularly important before the year 2000, before we started relying more heavily on DNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you. And speaking of DNA, could you briefly describe how DNA assists to identify the remains that you discover.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: DNA analysis is an analysis which has greatly helped identifications. When you have a good DNA findings, then your result is 99.99 per cent, and this is never contested by either the family or anybody else who might want to challenge your findings. Every person has a DNA which is unique, and only a twin can have the same DNA, and this is the only cause of problem. If we have twins with the same DNA image, then we have a problem. Otherwise, the DNA is unique. When it comes to mortal remains, we encounter a problem. Bones and teeth are the ideal material for taking DNA. If the bones and teeth are well preserved, and they do keep better than any other part of the body, we can take the DNA, but we don't know who that is, because this is still an unknown person. We have to move one step forward, and that DNA has to be compared with the next of kin. The DNA's taken from blood, usually from the mother or father of the missing person or the wife and the child of the missing person. This is what is done in paternity testing. In that same way, we prove who the father is or who the child is. If we have a mother and a father, then we take their DNA samples from living relatives, and if we have a missing son with his DNA taken from the bones, we can match the two and we can prove that that mother and that father are the parents of that missing person and that missing person cannot be anybody else but their son. The same applies to a situation where we're talking about a wife and a child. We actually proved that that child can only be the child of that mother and that late father and that's how we prove that the body belongs to that person. The DNA method is virtually perfect. However, there are cases when even the DNA method cannot be help, i.e., we will not be able to isolate the DNA from either the bones or the teeth. Usually we are talking about the bodies who have burnt. The DNA was disintegrated. It cannot be found in the bones. Or if the bodies were exposed to unfavourable conditions for a long time. For example, if they were in open air, then the bones disintegrate. They turn into dust and the DNA cannot be isolated. Unfortunately, we have cases in which we cannot identify the person either by the classical method or by the DNA analysis because simply DNA cannot be isolated in some cases. I have to say that the DNA analysis which is used -- which has been used since 1992, 1993, but it took off in a bigger way since 1999 and 2000. In Croatia we have three large laboratories. One of them is in Zagreb, and this is where routine identifications are performed. Today everybody that is found, that is processed is subject to the DNA analysis. So every identification process is completed with a full DNA analysis of that body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Strinovic, could I ask you to slow down a little bit. The interpreters have some difficulty to follow your speech. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you some questions now about the topic of cause of death that you mentioned, and I'll ask you about some of the factors that go into assessing cause of death. Firstly, how can the clothes that are found on a set of remains assist in establishing what the cause of death was?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to start by saying this: When it comes to establishing the cause of death in bodies which were found after a number of years is one of the most difficult tasks that faces a forensic expert. Believe me, it is very difficult to be decisive, and we like to be as sure as possible as when it comes to issues like that. When it comes to identifying post-mortem remains after a number of years, then the cause of death is a delicate issue and it is very difficult to be a hundred per cent sure. When it comes to clothes, obviously everything that is found around the body and on the body, everything that is damaged can help with arriving at a final conclusion on the cause of death. Every piece of clothing that can -- that is found on the dead body, if it covers that part of the body which was injured, then that item of clothing will be damaged. For example, if the body was killed by a projectile, that projectile will have damaged the skin, but it will also damage the clothes. Those are small defects on the clothes that suggest that the person died from a bullet. However, the clothes do not last long. They disintegrate, and after a while it is going to be more difficult to provide more concrete information based on the clothes. The clothes do help, and if we encounter characteristics damage on the clothes, we can use it to support our findings on the cause of that arrived at from the bones and from other tissues. We will be able to tell whether the person was -- died as a result of injuries or from some other causes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: What about the skull, cranium?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: The skull is something that in most cases when the skull is preserved tells us in the most exact way what the cause of death was, because of some specific features of the skull. If the skull is preserved, and we are talking only about the bones, you can see defects that are the imprints of the object that are used to inflict the injuries. There will be cuts or blunt imprints. If the body was injured by a projectile, we will find the entry and exit bounds on the cranium which are very characteristic. What does that mean? Every projectile, when it reaches a bone, it pierces the bone owing to its speed. However, where the place where it enters the bone is a round and regular defect and the exit wound will cause damages of the bone, so such injuries inflicted by a broad projectile are very characteristic. When a projectile exits the skull, the interior part is damaged to a lesser extent, and the exterior is damaged to a bigger extent. We can then therefore establish that it was a gun-shot wound. We can establish where the projectile entered the wound, where it existed the skull. The skull is obviously very interesting when it comes to identification but when it comes to the cause of death, it is very difficult when we have gun-shot wounds. The problem arises when a gun-shot wound which is very common is inflicted by a fast projectile. What does that mean? If a projectile travels fast we have an extensive wound of all the structures including bones. Why is that the case? Because we're talking about high velocity, high energy that is transferred onto the tissue, onto the bone and the kinetic energy is transformed into the elastic energy which injuries the tissues including the bones, and then at the end, after a while when the bone disintegrates, we end up with a skull which is fragmented, and it is very difficult for us to put the fragments together and to establish the true cause of death; i.e., it is very difficult to reconstruct that the person suffered from a gun-shot wound. A similar picture is seen in an explosion of a shell when there is shrapnel and the shrapnel destroys the bones -- bone, and there's also other type of trauma such as blunt trauma, several blows which injured the bone and once the muscles and the soft tissues disappear, what we end up with is a fragmented bone from which it is difficult to reconstruct how the injury was inflicted. I'm saying this just to make sure you understand that not all the injuries will be clear cut. In some cases it will be very clear what the cause of death was and sometimes it will not be possible to establish the cause of death for the reasons that I mentioned just a while ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And how do X-rays assist in establishing the cause of death?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: I must say that at the beginning of our work when it comes to the processing of mortal remains, we did not have an X-ray. It was obtained in 1986, and then we could put the bodies through the X-ray machine. Why is that important? Because it takes the image of the bones and all the other metal bodies -- metal objects on the body which are sometimes very difficult to find. Even when you're faced with a fresh body, sometimes it is impossible for us to find the projectile or shrapnel. We have to subject the body to an X-ray in order to localise the location of the metal and then we extract that metal object from the body. It is particularly obvious when the bodies have spent a lot of time in the soil, and by an external examination or if soft tissues are preserved, it is very difficult to establish the place where the projectile or a metal bullet is. So the only way to establish the location of such metal objects is -- or the fragments of -- or particles of metal is to use an X-ray machine. After we started using an X-ray machine, we could say with more certainty how the person was injured and what the cause of death was, especially when we were faced with shrapnel that can be lethal, and it was only in that way that we could positively conclude what happened to the person who died.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: So based on what you've told us, if we have an autopsy report where the cause of death says unknown or unascertained, is it possible that that person could still have been shot by a gun, for instance, but they cannot determine the precise cause of death?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so. I've tried to explain that. In some cases we have typical wounds of either soft tissues or the bones that remain. However, in some cases it is not the case. The wounds are not typical. There are no multiple fractures or multiple injuries, and we cannot draw a conclusion on the cause of death, although it does appear possible that the cause of death was a gun-shot wound, but it cannot be positively concluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could we now get 65 ter document 03005 on the monitor. Sorry, do I see that you have a question there before we move on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Before we move on, if I may. Witness, Mr. Strinovic, if I understood you properly, and you correct me if I am wrong, when we're talking about the skull, you said that a projectile, the faster it is, the easier it is to establish the cause of death. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct. In cases when such fast projectiles cause multiple fractures of the skull which is very common. If a projectile damages the skull in such a way that we do not have a typical entry-exit wound but only multiple fractures of the bones that are fractures, in such cases we cannot talk with certainty about the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Is that the same for soft tissues or is it different with soft tissues?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When a fast projectile reaches soft tissues, it goes through such soft tissues, and the faster the speed, the higher the speed, the bigger the destruction. A slow projectile that reaches soft tissue makes a canal that is of the diametre of the projectile. If we are talking about more than 800 or a thousand metres in a second then the damages of the soft tissue will be larger for the same reason it is the case with the bone. The kinetic energy of a fast projectile is transformed into the elastic energy that destroys tissue and creates a huge wave in the body which results in extensive injuries which are much larger than the projectile itself. That's the reason why fast projectiles are as dangerous as they are. They do not need to injure vital organs and still they can cause death because they cause may -- massive destruction of soft tissues, the traumatic shock, bleeding and ultimately a person's death.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. This was very clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And so is it correct to summarise that an injury inflicted by a slower projectile causing an entry wound and exit wound, for instance, to the skull, will be easier to ascertain the cause of death than if you have from a faster projectile which has shattered the skull? Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, you're right. This is precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Okay. Could we get 03005 on the monitor, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: This should come up on the monitor in front of you, Dr. Strinovic. Do you see this document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, if you're talking about my curriculum vitae, yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And does this document set out further details about your background, your education, your membership of expert associations and professional experience?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: It does, obviously. I drafted my own curriculum vitae, so it's truthful, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And then if we go on a couple of pages, we'll see discussions of your role in exhumations and identifications; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And does this report still accurately reflect the methodology that you used in the exhumations, autopsies, and identification processes that you were involved in?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd request that 65 ter document 03005 be admitted and that could be admitted publicly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit P351. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: I'm now going to ask some questions about the specific documents related to the victims in this case, and for the purposes of this, there is a table referring to a large number of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: We have printed out hard copies, colour copies of this for Your Honours and for the Defence. There is, in fact, two tables: One relating to all the incidents other than the Ovcara incident; and one relating to the Ovcara incident. With Your Honours' leave, I would distribute those to you as I think they'll be easier to use than if we were all trying to follow on the computer the whole time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please do, Mr. Gillett.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And while they're being distributed, I would point out that we're happy to provide searchable electronic copies of these tables to Your Honours and the Defence after the witness has testified. Also, these documents were made before we had 65 ter numbers, so the document numbers referred to in the table are the ERNs or doc IDs so I'll try and refer to the documents by those numbers as we go through this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Gillett, when you say searchable document, you mean Excel format?

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Excel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: So we're going to start with the thicker document, which is the non-Ovcara one. Now, Dr. Strinovic, in preparation for your testimony in this case today, were you asked to review a collection of exhumation, autopsy and identification related documents?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And does the table that is in front of you set out the references to the documents that you reviewed?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And I would just note that there are some additional documents referred to in the table that Dr. Strinovic was not asked to review. They are generally missing persons questionnaires, and the way that you can see that is if the column -- the box in the column document authenticity is blank, that means it is not a document that he was asked to review.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: If we look at the column entitled "Cause of death" which is the third from the right, does this list the causes of death for each victim that reflects the underlying documentation?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And when you carried out the process of reviewing these documents, if you concluded that one was authentic, did you cross out the "No" in the document "Authenticity" column and leave the "Yes" showing?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And where there is handwriting on this document, whose handwriting is that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: That's my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, when you carried out the review of all this documentation, on what basis were you able to authenticate the various documents in a general sense?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: My basis for comparison were the original autopsy protocols that were -- are kept at the forensic institute in Zagreb. When I compared the two, I could establish that we're talking about the same documents, i.e., I could establish the authenticity of the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And were you involved in producing some of these documents?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: If you mean autopsy reports, then yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And do you know the performers of the autopsy reports other than yourself that appeared on these documents?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think I can say I know all of them. They're my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're going to go through some examples. Obviously in the interests of time we won't be able to go through every single one, but I'll try and pick some emblematic ones that -- with some commonly occurring issues to help explain how the table works. Just as an aside, the letters SNS are written beside some of the documents. That's an internal thing that can be ignored. It just relates to a previous case. And where some documents are coloured yellow, that can also be ignored. It just relates to more recently received documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: If we go to page 1, the first entry is for paragraph 24, the first listed victim, and these victims follow the order in the annexes to the indictment. And the first lists victim is Zoran Andjal. The first document listed for this first victim is an autopsy report.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And if we could get that report on the screen, it is ERN 02027317, and that's 65 ter 03685. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, if we look at the persons that carried out this autopsy, do you recognise any of the names on page 1?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] That is Dr. Mladen Marcikic. His is head of the institute in Osijek.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And do you know the autopsy performer, Boris Dumencic?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course. He was also doing specialisation -- [Interpretation] He did his specialisation in Zagreb, and he worked in Osijek together with Dr. Marcikic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: The second sentence of text on the first page which starts "On 23 February, 1998," states that on LOK 1, under the number 152 in Celije, "exhumation of remains was carried out." What does this number 152 signify?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: When an exhumation is begun in a certain area, the site is mark such as it was done in Celije, and its divided into locations, location 1, 2, et cetera, whereas 152 is the number of the body bag where a certain person is placed. In fact, their mortal remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And what information does this report contain? Could you talk us just briefly and generally through the elements that it sets out?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: In this autopsy report we see first the description of the clothing together with all the objects found. If you want me, I can quote them here. We'll refer to it just in general terms. After that, we proceed with the autopsy itself, and we go part by part describing first - we can move to the next page - the head where multiple fractures were found of the head, followed by the lower and upper jaw and then other parts of the body. Do you want me to comment on this or --

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: No, that's okay. And then where would we find the cause of death for this victim listed?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: In the conclusion. The basic information about injuries is provided, and reference is made to a violent death.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And does that information in the conclusion about the injuries reflect what is in the table under the column "Cause of death" for Zoran Andjal?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In this table we see before us, we see injuries listed, and in view of their number and appearance, they indicate a high probability of a gun-shot or blast wound.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And on the report, if the victim were found with a weapon or a military ID, for example, would that also be listed on an autopsy or exhumation report?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: I must say that the pathologist, when he gets the body, he will describe the entire body, including with everything on it, and that includes weapons, and if there is nothing, he will just say the body is naked. But the person performing the autopsy describes everything that comes with the body.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Okay. On page 1 of this report, we don't necessarily need to go there, but it refers to a Iscan Yasar phase 4 reflecting an age of 26 to 32 years. What is this Iscan Yasar phase? Sorry, it's Iscan Yasar. Maybe we should go to page 1 of the report. It's the third line from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: I still don't see that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Apologies. It's in the Croatian original. I believe it is page 2. It is the third paragraph of text down.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: I can tell you the following: When you look at changes on the bones, you also look to see whether you can determine the age based on the bones. There are several methods to determine the age of a person, and one of them is the examination of ribs that grow into the sternum. With time changes occur in the ribs. First of all, in youth they are elastic and then they ossify and get less flexible. Anyway, you can see changes on the ribs that are due to age, and looking at the ribs you can give an estimate on the age. In this specific case, it was determined that this was a young person aged 26 to 32. That is an age where ossification is not complete. But these are normal changes that exist in every person, not with the same speed. In any case, you can see on certain bones such as the ribs and the pelvis or even the skull. When the person is still young, we can roughly estimate the age by the changes that occur on every bone.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And you're referred to the pelvis. In the following bullet point on the pelvis it refers to the Suchey-Brooksukoy test phase 3. Is this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gillett, before you go there, could you ask the witness what is -- ask again what Iscan Yasar means. According to Iscan Yasar -- I suppose it is the name of a method but we should have it on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could you clarify what Iscan Yasar means?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: According to Iscan Yasar, that means those are the authors who promoted this method, who concluded after examining many cases that there were certain changes that could indicate age and provided a table with -- with a range. Those are the authors of the method.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And in the following bullet point the report refers to the - forgive my pronunciation - Suchey-Brooksukoy phase 3. What is this?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: The situation here was very similar to the previous one. Those were authors who [indiscernible] the changes on the symphysis, which is the joint between the left and the right side of the pelvis. First of all, these bones have cartilage and they are elastic. Later with age they lose their elasticity and ossify. So persons can be divided by age groups. Here it was determined that the age would be 21 to 46 years. This is rather a large range, but it's not considered to be a very precise method.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could we move to the second document for this same listed victim in the indictment which is ERN 06822903, and that's 65 ter 3686.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gillett, I think the best thing to do is the take the first break now, even if we started 15 minutes late, but we -- this way we won't get confused. Mr. Witness, we take the break now for half an hour and come back at 11.00. The usher will escort you out of court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gillett, while we are waiting for the witness, I could perhaps ask you this -- ask to clarify that eventually with the witness. Page 86 and 87, in the last column there is a handwritten note, and it says "CD correct," what that would mean. And at page 88 and 89, it is said "No protocol."

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: That is certainly on my list of questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Welcome back, Dr. Strinovic. Thank you. Now, we were just looking at the second document for the first listed victim on the non-Ovcara table, and this is Zoran Andjal. So I believe this document is still up on the screen in front of you. Could you tell us what this document is?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's a death certificate. It is a document issued to the family after an identification is definitively confirmed, and when the family agrees with the identification, it signs to confirm that it is precisely their relative, and then with this death certificate they go to the municipality where the body was found and they get the final death certificate as the final document confirming death.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: On this document, in box number 3 on the first page, the date of death is recorded as 22 September 1991. What would that information or that date be based on?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: It's probably clear to you that we don't know the exact time of death, but we must have some information. We get that information usually from the family or from the government commission which indicate as a rule the date of disappearance, which is sometimes probably the date of death. Otherwise, the date of death is difficult to determine. So we take that date to be the date of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And so am I right thinking that they are not always accurate and certain dates of death?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. That's what I just said. We really don't know, because we were not eyewitnesses. We can only assume based on other information such as information about the time when the person went missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: What about the place of death that's recorded? Would that be based on the same type of information?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: The same. The fact is that the place where the body was found is taken to be the place of death. Of course, it doesn't have to be necessarily so, but in absence of other information, the date -- the place where the body was found is taken as the place of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And this may be an obvious question, but if you did have a witness to the event or someone with specific information as to the place or time of death, that would be reflected in the death certificate if they had provided that information?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: I think that would be written.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Okay. If we could move to the third document for this victim, Zoran Andjal. This is ERN -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gillett, I have a question about this last question and answer. Mr. Strinovic, you say, "I think that would be written." What would be written? Would be written the date of death that you get from that information or would it be written that there is information as to such and such date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand the question, but it's difficult to give a definitive answer. As I said, we usually put the date when the person went missing in these death certificates. If there were witnesses who knew more about the events and dates, it was possible to enter such information in the death certificate as well, but I don't know really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: If we could shift to the third document for this victim, and this is ERN 06822905. That's 65 ter 03687. And this is a DNA report.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: You've already described the general process of DNA identification so I won't go back over that in any detail, but I'd note that the -- this report refers to the body number 152 from Celije, which is the same number that we've just seen on the first document above. On page 1, the last line of text, and this is in the English, it concludes that this was most probably Zoran Andjal. On what basis do they conclude that this is Zoran Andjal, or most probably?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: It's the usual language involving DNA. When we talk about 99.99 per cent, that is the statistical expression that is almost certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could we go to the second page of this document, if there is a second page. Okay. And the very last block of text under "Opinion," is that where we find the percentage that you've just referred to?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As we see at the end of this opinion there is a percentage, 99.9998 per cent. That is the degree of probability that this is indeed the named person. It is a statistical expression for almost practically certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Where do we find the people that samples were taken from to compare with the remains to establish who this person was?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: In this specific case blood samples were given by the mother and the father, and this proves paternity. It proves that the person found was indeed the child of these two persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And I saw you pointing to the screen. Were you pointing to the heading "Findings" on this -- on this document?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: In the opinion I read the percentage. In the findings above, there is information about the parents.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I'm going to turn now to the entry for the victim called Ivan Zelember which is on page 5 of the table. And this -- the document that I'd like to look at on the screen is 65 ter 03709. This is the first document listed, the autopsy report for this victim on page 5. Now, while we wait for this document to come up, I'd note that on page 3, under the conclusion, it refers to fracture to the right side of the face bone -- or fractures, sorry, to the right side of the face bone, right upper jaw, and left side of the scapula and left arm. This is on the document on page 3. Page 3 of the English. Now, these -- these various fractures, do you see that in front of you on the document on the screen, not on the -- I believe it's also reflected in the table, but on the document on the screen?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could these injuries have been caused by a simple accident, for instance, falling over or something like that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Injuries such as those listed and described in view of their localisation and juxtaposition indicate the use of force rather than fall. In a fall, the juxtaposition of injuries would be a little different, and it would involve some injuries that are not listed here. These injuries are typical for the use of a blunt instrument or perhaps the palm of a hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: What is it about the localisation and juxtaposition of these injuries that makes them more typical of injuries from a blunt instrument than a fall, for instance?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, there are two injuries to the upper jaw, and the maxial bone that regularly occur from a blow. In a fall, injuries would be most frequent to the back of the head. When somebody falls on their face, it is to be expected the nose and the forehead would be injured, and it would have to be a very bad fall. So the injuries juxtaposed as here are typical for a blow. There is also an injury to the shoulder blade which occurs from a blow. In a fall forward, there would be injuries to the lower jaw and the forehead. The shoulder blade would not be injured. And it's not typical for a fall. This specific injury to the shoulder blade is difficult to sustain from things other than a blow.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could I turn now to page 25 of the table, and this is the entry for Pero Rasic. Sorry, sorry, not page 25, page 14 of the table. This is Pero Rasic, who is one of the victims listed in paragraph 25 of the indictment. Now, the first thing for this victim, in the indictment he's listed as Petar Rasic, but in the documents he's listed as Pero Rasic. How could that come about?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: I can only say that Petar and Pero is one and the same thing. It's one and the same name, which can be interpreted in two different names -- or, rather, expressed in two different ways. This is a legitimate mistake. It's actually the same name spelled in two different ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, for this victim we have an autopsy report carried out in 2002 in Croatia, and we also have an attached earlier autopsy report carried out on 16 October, 1991, and how does it come about that you have two autopsy reports carried out in two different countries 20 years apart?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: It's not the only case. In this situation, the body that was found on the banks of the Danube near Novi Sad was transferred and processed in Novi Sad. That was in 1991. After that, the body was buried as an unknown individual, and it was only much later that that body was finally recognised based on a sample of the bone that was taken for the DNA analysis. It was then transferred to Croatia. Another post-mortem was carried out 20 years later, as you have stated it yourself, and finally the person was recognised, identified, and buried under his name, and the whole process was thus finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: In the earlier autopsy report from Novi Sad, and this can be found at page 14 of 65 ter document 3755, so perhaps we could get that on the screen to show it as I describe it, but I'll summarise that the autopsy report from 1991 notes that the body had the tattoo of a flying bird on the left arm with a date underneath it stating 13.IX.1966, and the inscription JNA. It also notes that one of the teeth was made of yellow metal and that there was a ring with the body. This is all shown on, I believe, page 14. Now, are these the types of elements that could assist with identifying a victim?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Very much so. The information listed in here, and this information obviously was obtained not long after the body was found, a tattoo can help a lot when it comes to the identification of a person.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: So if these would have assisted with the identification, why were the earlier reports carried out in Serbia not handed over earlier?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's a very difficult question and a question that is very difficult to answer. There is an explanation. This person was treated as an unknown person. That's how he was buried. His body was found on the banks of the Danube, one could assume where the person was from, but obviously it took some time to co-ordinate matters, to exchange mortal remains and for everyone to finalise such cases. We're talking about various kinds of circumstances including political circumstances and all sorts of misunderstandings. All of that played a role in the duration of the process.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And could I ask you to clarify "political circumstances." I understand there are a number of different factors, but if you could just explain what you mean by that term.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: What I meant was that there was no goodwill in place for exchanges to take place, for the truth to be established, to establish why those people were killed, who they were at the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Okay. And I'll be returning to this topic in relation to Ovcara subsequently in the examination. For now, if we could turn to -- sorry, page 34 of the table, and this is the entry for Josip Bence. And if we could get document 65 ter 03856 on the screen, page 2. Now, on page 2 of this document, for the cause of death it first states a Latin term which I believe is vulnera sclopetaria capitis -- it should be on page 2. Vulnera sclopetaria capitis. Subsequently, it says the cause of death was war. Firstly, what does vulnus sclopetaria capitis mean? And secondly, why would it state cause of death is war?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Vulnera sclopetaria capitis is a gun-shot wound to the head. And as for your second question about the war, I must say that it is an administrative worker at the institute who fills out the form, and sometimes when causes of death were entered were not the strict translation of what is here. Like for example here it says vulnera sclopetaria capitis. Instead, somebody entered the word "war," meaning the person died in the war. That's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: I believe if we shift over to page 2 of the English, it will show that description where it lists war. I apologise. This may be a doc -- ah, yes. Sorry. There it is under the data of violent death and it says external cause of violent depth equals war. It's on page 2 of the English. Now aside from various discrepancies in names that may arise, in some of these documents, as you've noted on the table, there are discrepancies in the dates of birth between the dates of birth listed in the indictment and dates of birth listed in the documents. How could this arise that you would have different dates of birth provided?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Obviously this depends on the source of information. The information about any sorts of dates is obtained from various people, including family members such as mothers, wives, and sometimes they provide us with different dates. We must have obtained this information from somebody. We did not make it up. The information was obtained from somebody, and sometimes discrepancies are possible, but they should be attributed to the various sources of the information obtained.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And for the record, one example where we have this is Ivan Palijan on page 27 of the report where the indictment lists him as born in 1956, but Dr. Strinovic has marked in the table that his birth date is 1949. That's page 27 of the table. Now, if we skip to page 85 of the table, near the end, the entry for Helena Albert says protocol missing, and then words to the effect of the documents on the CD appear correct. What does this mean?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I could not follow you. Let's repeat. We're talking about page 85?

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: 85. Sorry. In the last column, "Additional comments," the handwritten words say "protocol missing. Documents on CD appear correct." Could you explain what this means? It's for the first entry on that page, Helena Albert.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Helena Albert, yes. This means that we do not have the post-mortem protocol. It was not available to us when we drafted our report. As for what we received from you on CD, that seems to be a correct finding.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And when you say "a correct finding," did you review the documents that were on the CD in this instance for Helena Albert?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That -- that's what it means.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And I note there are similar handwritten words in the entries on page 86 for Viktorija Albert and page 87 for Ana Terzic. Your Honour also noted at two instances where the additional comments record no protocol, and in the document authenticity column for those two documents Dr. Strinovic has indicated no. utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, moving to the entries that the President referred to where it stated "No protocol," the first one is on page 88 of the table, and it's in relation to Stevan Nad. utterances.text: And if we go to the final page, which I believe is page 2, and look at the stamp and signature. Perhaps on -- at the end of -- if we go one -- one further page. Do you recognise the signature and/or stamp there of Dr. Marcikic?

utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And you've had a chance to review this document during proofing. Does it appear to be an authentic autopsy report?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a kind of an autopsy report that Dr. Marcikic used to draft, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Okay. If we could shift across the page in the table to the very final page, 89, and for the first victim named under Vlahovic, again we see "No protocol" listed. So could we bring up 65 ter 04183, which is ERN 02008479. And this is again an autopsy report, and it indicates it's carried out by Dr. Mladen Marcikic. If we could go to the signature on this document on the final page, and you could take a look. Do you recognise his signature and/or stamp on this document?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, like in the previous case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And when you looked at the document during proofing, was there anything that would suggest it's not an authentic autopsy report?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: No. I would say that this is an example of a very typical autopsy report drafted by Dr. Marcikic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: If we return to page 1 of this same document on the monitor, the autopsy report, it describes defects to the cranium with what appears to be an entry wound from the bullet in the occipital region and an exit wound in the temporal region. That's on page 1 in the English version. And it's in the block of text which is in the middle of the page starting with the word "Head." So where we have what appears to be an entry wound from a bullet in the occipital region, an exit wound in the temporal region, how can the examiner tell which one is the entry wound and which one is the exit wound?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: I have already explained when I spoke about the cranium, i.e., the skull. If we're dealing with a projectile, we can establish the exact entry point as well as the exact exit point when we look at the fracture of the skull. The entry wound is smaller. The exit wound is bigger. We can establish the direction. The interior defect is smaller of the exit wound, and the funnel is turned differently. So when you have a gun-shot wound through the cranium, we can establish with an absolute certainty which one is the entry wound and which one is the exit wound.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And if I'm correct, the entry in the occipital region is at the back, and the exit wound is at the front. What would this suggest about the way in which this victim and other victims with similar injuries died?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: We can look at this situation in two ways. In any case when the entry wound is at the back and when the direction is either lateral or towards the front, this shows the position of the head when the shot was fired. In this case, the back of the head was before the gun, and this is typical of executions when bullets are fired in the back of the head. It -- the situation could have been different, of course. That person may have found himself in that position, i.e., the gun from which fire was opened could have been pointed into the back of the person's head by accident.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Okay. Your Honours, at this point we would tender these two -- these two documents, which are 04181 and 04183 for admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Okay. The first name listed here at number 1 is Zoran Andjal, who we've discussed earlier, and if we look at the information for Zoran Andjal, what does this document -- what information does it provide in relation to him?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: I'm very sorry. The print is so small that I cannot read it. Could you help me in any way? Could you zoom in a little to make it more legible? Now it's better. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: You want an explanation for Zoran Andjal. You want me to say what information is provided about him; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Particularly in the column "Remarks."

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: It begins with the mass grave Celije, exhumation date 23 February 1998. That person was put in body bag 152, and it was identified on the 3rd of November, 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Then if we look further down at entry number 12 for Ernest Baca, it says in the remarks column "Taken over from Republic of Serbia." What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: When the exchanges began and we were able to recover the bodies that were buried in Serbia as often happened in Novi Sad, for instance, Croatia took them over. In this case this was 23rd February, 2002, and it was identified on the 23rd of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Yes. And -- sorry, if he could just check those dates, and this is for entry number 12 taken over --

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Am I correct to understand it was taken over from Serbia on 21st of March, 2002, and identified on 12th of February, 2003?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
