utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: 12.15, Mr. Gillett.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: 12.15. Okay. Could we now get document 06365 on the monitor. 06365. And this is one of the documents that was added to the 65 ter list at the start of proceedings today, as are the following three documents that I'm going to address.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: At the top of page 1 of this document, it states -- it's record 858/91 for an unidentified person. So who created this autopsy report or protocol?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: It's obviously a report written in 1991, and considering the way it was written, I suppose it was written in Serbia. I don't know exactly where. Not yet. Maybe we'll be able to see where the autopsy was performed. Anyway, it was performed in 1991. The body was found in the Danube, so I suppose it was in Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And have you seen similar documents to this?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, under the heading "Autopsy" on page 2 of this document, the findings indicate that the person was shot in the head but was alive when they landed in the water of the Danube. How could the examiner conclude that the person was still alive when they were thrown into the Danube?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When injury occurs, including injuries to the head, death does not have to occur immediately. Death occurs even after a gun-shot wound, after some time, sometimes even hours. However, when the body finds itself in water, lungs continue to breathe, and in autopsy you can establish the cause of death easily by seeing whether the water reached the lungs, the alveoli, or another part of the lungs. So we can conclude in this case that the person was wounded in the head, came into contact with water and died from drowning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would seek to admit this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit P355. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: If we could now get 65 ter document 06366 on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, this is a DNA analysis. If you take a look at the document, could you tell us who carried it out.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: This analysis was performed in the hospital in Osijek, and it was done by the doctor who still performs DNA analysis today.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And in the previous document we saw the number at the top 858/91, but it was an unidentified person. How can we link this autopsy report with this -- that -- that previous -- sorry. How could we link this DNA report with the previous autopsy report?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: There is a link with a number from Novi Sad, 858/91. That's the number of -- on one side on the autopsy report from the autopsy done in Novi Sad, and this link, which is the number of body bag in the report, and this indicates a connection. Those are the samples from that body bag, so it's a sample from that person.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would seek the admission of this document at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit P356. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could we now get document 06367.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And when you take a look, could you describe what this document is and who it's for.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] I'm sorry. [Interpretation] Could we enlarge it? Thank you very much. This is a death certificate that we discussed before. It's an official document stating that a person has been identified, and this certificate is given to the family. This concerns Ivan Tomicic. Place of death, Dalj, municipality Erdut. Do you want to know anything else from this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: That's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: We would seek the admission of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit P357. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we get document 06368, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, you had a chance to review this document during proofing. Could you describe to us what it is and let us know if we need to enlarge it for you.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember this case. We discussed it before. In cases where we have a missing person, if they are not found and identified after a certain period, whereas there are witnesses and there is firm evidence that the person is dead, then before a court in the municipality of residence of that person proceedings are conducted to have the court issue a decision, a ruling, that that person is dead. That is done when the person has been missing for a long time and there are witnesses who can confirm that the person is dead, although there are cases where the family has received a death certificate and the person is later found and identified by name and surname. Then another procedure is conducted when the initial certificate is used to obtain a final confirmation of death, final certificate.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And is this decision, from what you've reviewed, an authentic decision, and who is it for? Who is the victim?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: I see the Croatian coat of arms. It looks authentic. It says it's the Municipal Court in Beli Manastir, and the decision is issued declaring dead Tibor Siles, born in Osijek on 23rd May, 1963.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: I'd seek the admission of this document at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit P358. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, I'm now going to turn to the Ovcara incident, which is paragraph 32 of the indictment, and so this is discussed -- or reflected in the smaller of the two tables that was distributed. I'd recall at the outset that this incident is covered by a number of the agreed facts between the parties, and those are facts 103 to 110, where it's been agreed essentially, I'm summarising, that the 194 named victims in the annex for paragraph 32 of the indictment were murdered at Ovcara, that they were detained when they were murdered, that they were buried in a mass grave at Ovcara, that the grave was protected by UN personnel, and the exhumation and autopsies were carried out by international and domestic experts, and representatives the Croat and Yugoslav authorities were present.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: In the process of examinations and identifications of the people found at Ovcara, what was your involvement?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: I'll have to provide an introduction, because it is a very peculiar case, and I was involved from the early days in the investigation concerning Ovcara and retrieving the bodies from Ovcara. As I said before, in the month of December 1991, I was invited to join the commission for detained and missing persons, which was just being established, and it was to deal with all the missing persons in Croatia, but one of the major issues were the persons who went missing at the hospital in Vukovar. The whole country was seeking answers. It happened on the 9th of November, 1991, and ever since that time there was an outcry for the truth to be revealed and to find out what happened to these people. So starting in January 1992, we had negotiations between Croatia and Serbia, also involving international organisations, and the main issues were related precisely to the people removed from the Vukovar Hospital. So I was involved from the very beginning. I know the chronology of the inquiry into Ovcara, and I -- if you wish, we can discuss that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I just noted -- I just noted an error in transcript at page 51, line 2, about the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: On the record it says 9 November 1991, for when the commission was established. Is that correct or could you give us the correct date?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: I must be honest, I don't know exactly when the commission is first mentioned with the date, but I know that I was invited to join it in November. Whether it was earlier, I can't say with certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, he didn't speak about the commission, the date of founding of the commission, but about the disappearance of the patients from the Vukovar Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, sorry, for clarifying that. I'll be asking some further questions about the details of the incident subsequently, so we'll come back to this topic, and at that point I think it will be clarified. So apologies to confuse the two issues there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: For a start, if we can look to the table that's been distributed, and I'll ask you similar questions as to the previous table without going into as much detail in light of the agreed facts, but in preparation for your testimony today, were you asked to review autopsy reports or records for the victims at the Ovcara incident?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did that several times, and I prepared for this case in the same way, comparing reports, autopsy reports with the tables that were presented to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And were you able to authenticate these documents?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I did, and every page has been signed by me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And in the column called "ID Method," which is the fifth column from the right, it refers to classical and DNA. What -- does this relate to your previous answers about the means of identifying victims?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. We could talk about that a lot, but in any case, we began with Ovcara. From a classification the DNA analysis had not been perfected at that time, so the first cases were identified in the traditional way, comparing the ante-mortem information with findings, and that was accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And if we could open the first document referred to here, which is for Josip Kozul and the document ERN is 00559729. That number is 00559729. And does this report set out the typical elements that you would find in an autopsy report, from your experience?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I would say it's a very good report, including all the information that is established in this type of autopsy. So it's a job very well done.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And then if we could go to the next page, please. It says at the first word "Commingling: No." What does "commingling" mean? It's the very first word at the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Maybe if we could get the B/C/S copy of this for that first word. There is no B/C/S? To explain, these documents are -- we broke out the translations from a much bigger B/C/S document, and which I believe should be available on e-court under 00559729 to 00560697, but I can actually get the 65 ter number for you. Yeah. The 65 ter number is 4192.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could I ask without referring to the document, are you aware of the term "commingling"?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. In that context, it means mixing, commingling. That is a frequent problem with mass graves, and we have to be very careful with this commingling. We have to separate one body from another completely. In some situations such as wells, it is practically impossible, but in mass graves such as Ovcara through careful examination of mortal remains it is possible to finally separate one body from another and to avoid commingling.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, the autopsy reports for these victims are quite formulaic, so I'm not going to go through more of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: I will ask do you know the approximate age range of the victims that were found at the Ovcara grave site?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember the range was 16 to 71 years -- sorry, 72 years. And it is rather precise because this is information we got after identification. In the course of processing, the anthropologist can give a rough estimate of the age based on the teeth, ribs, and the pelvis, and the estimate comes in a range. However, when we finalise the process and the body's identified, when we know the date of birth of that person, of course we know the exact age. This is why this range which I just mentioned, 16 to 72 years, was the final information after all the identifications were done.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And on the table where there is handwriting, is that your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is my handwriting and my signature at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And in some cases have you indicated where there are discrepancies in the dates of birth or spellings of names and marked the correct spelling or date of birth?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. If we leaf through the table for Ovcara, we'll see there are cases when the date of birth has been changed or the name, which is obviously a result of the final identification when we were able to put in the exact data.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: At this stage we'd ask for the table and the underlying documents to be admitted. Those are the documents with yes or no -- well, with yes indicated in the authenticity column, the final column. There are some missing persons questionnaires right at the end of the table which we are not admitting and they're blank in that authenticity column.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gillett, may I take it that in the Excel version you will add the 65 ter numbers of all these documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: We do indeed already have a version with the 65 ter numbers added, but they weren't available at the stage when we first made these.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And to -- just a couple of notes to tidy up in the remaining seconds. I'll just note with the handwritten remarks sometimes they're slightly difficult to make out, but I've confirmed with the witness that in the entry for Anton Mutvar the -- it should read "30.1.69." For the entry for OVC-004, the handwriting should read "13.6.1959." For the entry for OVC-066 the handwriting reads Holjevac that is with one L. For OVC-073 it reads "1.NOV.1979". And then I think the rest of the entries will be -- will be clear enough. We'll also note in the electronic versions of these tables the diacritics are not included, because if they're included it makes it hard to electronically search for the names. So that's the way it's set up. I see we've reached 12.15. Perhaps it's a good time to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gillett. Mr. Witness, we will take the second break now and come back at 12.45. The Court Usher will escort you out of court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Gillett.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Dr. Strinovic, before the break we were discussing the victims exhumed at Ovcara, and could I ask you how many bodies in total were exhumed from the Ovcara mass grave?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Exactly 20 bodies. I apologise, 200 bodies were exhumed at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And were all of the bodies or have all of the bodies been identified?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: No. We were in charge of that identification right from the very beginning, and we know that so far a total of 193 persons have been identified. One was identified based on the DNA, but that was not accepted by the family, which means that officially we have 192 bodies positively identified, 1 pending acceptance by the family, and 7 bodies pending identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could we get 65 ter document 02498 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, on this list we see a series of numbers, OVC-001, OVC-002 listed, and there are 200 of these numbers which corresponds to the total number of 200 bodies that you just provided. On page 1, if we look down to OVC-011, what see the words "No name." What does this mean?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: This means that OVC-011 has not been identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And if we shift to page -- page 3 of this document, after the list of 200 remains with OVC numbers -- if we could go one further page on, please. Sorry, and even one further beyond that. So there we see up to OVC-200, and after that we have six names listed which say "Not deceased." Could you explain who these people are or how this came about?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: These are people who were at Ovcara, but they were not killed there, which means that they are still alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Following the six names with "Not deceased" listed after them, we have another series of names, approximately 50 or 60, that continue across to the next page. Do you know the circumstances of these people or how these names arrived on this list?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: When people went missing from the Vukovar Hospital, lists of the missing persons were compiled. Those included the 200 bodies from Ovcara. However, the final list was longer, so the number of people missing from the hospital was about 260. The persons whose names are listed here are the persons who were on the list of the missing persons who were not found -- or, rather, whose bodies were not found at Ovcara but were originally on the list of the persons missing from the Vukovar Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And have efforts continued to locate those persons since the lists were originally created?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Of course we are trying. We have been trying from the very start to find all of those who are on the list. We will never stop looking for those people. To this very day we have not been fully successful in finding all the people from the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: We would seek the admission of this document at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit P359. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Dr. Strinovic, before the break you said that you would be able to provide a chronology of the investigation into the Ovcara incident and the mass grave. Could you briefly do so now.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: From the moment when people went missing from the Vukovar Hospital between the 19th and 20th December 1991, the list of their names was compiled and attempts were made to learn the truth. There were witnesses. There was indicia and indications that people from the hospital were taken in an unknown location after which their traces were lost. We held several meetings with the representatives of Serbia in order to try and learn as to what had happened to the people from the Vukovar Hospital. All that time from the moment those people went missing to the moment the grave was found and bodies there identified, we were very busy trying to establish the truth. According to the chronology, on the 20th of December, 1991 -- or, rather, in 1992, Dr. Clyde Snow, who was invited by the government of the Republic of Croatia and who arrived from the United Nations as an expert to try and locate the grave where the mortal remains were buried. He arrived in East Slavonia, and sometime in the month of November, as far as I can remember, he did go to the location. He found something that he found suspicious and indicative. He found an area which differed from the rest of the terrain. It was somewhat depressed. He found some traces of bullets there, and on the surface of the soil he found remains of human bones, and that was his first visit to Ovcara, and that was the first time that he indicated that the mass grave could be located there. That was in 1992. And then in 1993, we revisited that place. The grave was marked somewhat better and some trial excavations were done in 1993. The size of the grave was already defined by then, and then the exhumation of the grave had to start. Some preparations were already underway, but all the works were stopped, and what we could do at that moment, from the moment Clyde Snow visited the grave, further on the grave was secured by UNPROFOR soldiers. The area was well protected, so that in 1993, UNPROFOR soldiers were there, protect -- they protected the grave and practically we could not reach it until the year 1996. And then in the month of September of 1996, preparations started, followed by the exhumations of the grave at Ovcara. I was involved in all that as a monitor on the Croatian side, and on the Serbian side there were also experts hailing from Vukovar. Everything was observed. Everything was monitored while the exhumation of the mortal remains was carried out, and it was carried out by international experts who had prepared the exhumation. They carried it out, and the total of 200 bodies were found. Those bodies were bagged and marked with numbers 1 to 200. Number 1 was the first body that was found. Number 200 was the last that was found. All the bodies were brought to the surface and brought to Zagreb in a convoy to the school of medicine there at the institute for pathology. Special rooms were dedicated to the process of identification, the process of -- started sometime in late October 1996, and by the end of the year, the processing of the mortal remains was completed. Again, international experts were monitored by the Croatian side, the Serbian side, and the local authorities in Vukovar, which means that we had control of all what was being done. When the bodies were processed sometime in early 1997, we took over the bodies. We received the minutes of the post-mortem examinations about the part that was important for identification. We were under a lot of pressure. We had to proceed with identification as soon as possible, so we received the minutes of the post-mortem findings that helped us with the identification. We did not receive the part that dealt with the causes of death. The process of identification started. There was some cases which were identified based on the comparison of ante-mortal and post-mortem information, and in that way we managed to identify a certain number of cases which were relatively clear cut and simple. The families were invited to come to the institute of forensic medicine in Zagreb, and the process was launched. The identification was gradual. And let me just illustrate how painstakingly long the process was. Two weeks ago, we identified body number 192. This means that constantly from 1997 until this very day, we have been involved in trying to identify all the 200 bodies. We are still missing seven. So the process has been continuous. During the first couple of years, we used the method of classical identification, i.e., the comparison of post-mortem remains and ante-mortem information with the help of the families who kept on coming with new information, new photos, new details. We carried out our identification so that about 97 persons were identified in the classical way. And after that --

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: If I could just ask you to slow down slightly for the interpreters. Sorry, please just finish off what you were saying.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: So now we are at the end of this classical identification method by which we identified 97 persons, and then we could use the DNA method. All the other Ovcara cases have been identified using the DNA method so that we now have 192 positive identifications, 192 positive identifications plus the one that has not been accepted by the family for emotional reasons. And this is the most important thing that I can tell you about the chronology. From the very beginning, from the moment when the people went missing to this very -- if you need additional clarifications, or if there's anything else you'd like to ask me, I would be very happy to answer you, any questions you might have.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: I do have some clarifying questions. Going back to the start of the chronology, before the break you referred to the incident where the people were taken from the Vukovar Hospital and on the transcript it recorded the date 9 November 1991. Now, a few minutes ago when you gave a date it came out as 19 and 20 December 1991. Do you recall which month it was, November or December 1991? I realise that you weren't present at the incident.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: It's a memorable -- memorable date. It is the date when Vukovar fell. It was the 19th of November, 1991. That's the day when Vukovar fell and when the hospital fell into the hands of the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you. And then shifting in the chronology, you mentioned that in 1993, the initial exhumation that had been started was stopped. Who stopped the exhumation in 1993?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: According to what I know, the exhumation was indeed stopped in 1993 for political reasons, i.e. -- I don't know why exactly. I suppose that somebody else will know why it was stopped, but from what we knew at the time and from what we understood about why the exhumation was not being carried out was the large number of dead who all had come from one hospital, and I suppose that must have been the reason why the whole procedure was stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Who stopped the procedure?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: I repeat, I don't know. I can only assume. I can repeat what I've just told you. Obviously, the procedure was stopped by the people, by the authorities that were in power at the time, and that was not Croatia at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: The -- could you clarify which authorities you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the local Serbs and the former JNA held the power in their hands at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned that you don't know precisely why it was stopped, but you referred to political reasons. Can you elaborate on that at all?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: No, I can't speak about political reasons. I am not a politician. I can only speculate. If a large people went missing from a hospital, if they were obviously killed and buried somewhere, it was a delicate situation, and in 1993, the time was not ripe to publicise the whole matter, and I suppose that's why the whole procedure was stopped. But these are my speculations. Political reasons in this case may be at least one part of the answer to your question, but I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: That's totally understandable. Going back to the exhumations themselves, was the delay from 1993 until 1996 when the full exhumation was carried out, what effect did that delay have on the process of identifying the victims? I.e., did it make it easier for more difficult?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: As I've already stated, in 1993 the exhumation was stopped; i.e., no excavation was carried out, and nothing was happening in the area until 1996. It was guarded, and that's important. And obviously as time went by, the elements that help the identification deteriorated. The fresher the mortal remains, the better identification and the better establishment of the cause of death. And the longer the period of time between the death and the identification process, the more difficult it is to identify the body, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, you referred to the incident where the people were taken from Vukovar Hospital and that -- that you learned of this quite soon after it occurred. How did you learn about it, from what sources?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: There were several sources. The first source were newspapers and newspaper articles about the situation and about the people who went missing, and there were also reports received from the doctors who worked at the hospital, Dr. Bosanac and Dr. Njavro, one a surgeon and the other the hospital principal. They kept on sending us information. That information reached our commission, the commission that I was a member of. So those were the two principal sources, the media and the information that reached us from the Vukovar Hospital. Later on, we also received information from the relatives and the friends of the deceased of those who had gone missing. They wanted to know what had happened to them. And I apologise, maybe I should add one more thing. At that time, some people who were at Ovcara, the Croats who were supposed to be executed but escaped, they also provided some information when they arrived in Zagreb. I don't know when that was. I believe that it was very soon after the event, but they also testified as to what might have happened at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And you mentioned that information reached your commission and the commission was established in December 1991. Who did your commission meet with?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: That commission met with their counterparts from Serbia, a similar commission from Serbia, and those meetings were organised through international organisations that chaired those meetings. Those meetings were in English, and they were co-ordinated by those international organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And what subjects were discussed at those meetings between the two commissions?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: When those meetings started, we started by discussing people who went missing from Croatia and those that went missing from occupied areas. Each side had its arguments. We all looked for people who went missing and we couldn't find, and that's how we tried to learn from the other side and vice versa. The commission from Serbia sought information about those people who either went missing or of whom it was positively known that they had been killed during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could we get document 01161 on the monitor, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, this document on the front is titled "Draft. Minutes commission for Vukovar, Budapest, 12 June 1992." If we turn across to page 2, we see a list of participants in this meeting. Aside from yourself, obviously, can you describe who these people were and particularly the members of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia commission, as far as you recall.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the Croatian side there was Ivan Simonovic, law professor. There was Dr. Vesna Bosanac who was the CO of the Vukovar Hospital. Dubravka Horvat from the Red Cross of Croatia and Ivan Kopjar who represented the Armija, the Croatian Army, I believe. On the Serbian side I don't know much about those people. It was a long time ago. I never had any subsequent contacts with them. My colleague Dr. Stankovic was a captain at the time, and later was promoted to become a general. I know him. He was resident in Zagreb. That's how I knew him. And as for the others, I don't know. I don't want to guess. In any case, there were corresponding profiles to our side. There was the Red Cross, the organisation representing missing persons, the army, but I don't know any details about any of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Okay. If we turn to page 4 of the English under heading number 2. In the first line of the first paragraph under that heading we see that Dr. Strinovic said that: "It was necessary to establish a tripartite commission for the identification of mortal remains. At the meeting in Pec held in January, it was agreed that such commission would be formed. However, in Geneva, the Serbian side refused such co-operation. Up to date such commission has not been established." Do you recall making this suggestion for a tripartite commission?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: It was really a long time ago. What comes to mind first is this tripartite commission which was supposed to comprise the Croatian side, the Serbian side, and the international side. That would have been that tripartite commission, and that's what I had in mind when I proposed that, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And did they give reasons where the Serb side, where they did not agree to this co-operation?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: It's very hard for me to answer that question. I really don't know what the reason was. There may have been several, but I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: On page 7 of the English -- and this should be the second last paragraph from the end. It's page 6, last paragraph in the B/C/S version. Now, this is quite hard to read. Unfortunately, this is the only copy of this document we have. We checked. But in this paragraph at least that can be read, it states that: "Colonel Starcevic said that the JNA evacuated 174 persons and handed them to the CEE without precise names. According to Major Sljivancanin, among these 174 persons were all the wounded and ill from the hospital. The group stayed overnight at Ovcara and were handed the next day to the ECMM." Do you recall this account being given about missing persons from the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: What I remember, although it was a long time ago, was that the negotiations was very hard, and precisely from the example you cited, you can see that it was practically impossible. We did not get any reliable information, especially about Ovcara. About Ovcara we got nothing. So these negotiations were very difficult, and there was practically no progress on some important things such as Ovcara was for Croatia. One side would present very high figures, the other side would present very lower figures for the same thing, and we could not find common ground on -- on major issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honours, we'd seek admission of this document 01161.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit P360. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And if we could now get 65 ter 02444, and this is a photo booklet relating to the exhumation at Lovas farm, which is one of the -- relates to one of the incidents in the indictment. I believe it's paragraph 33 of the indictment. Now, if we could skip to the second picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: In this photo booklet, there is a large number of pictures. During proofing, did you have the opportunity to go through all of these pictures?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: So I'm not going to run through all of them, as similar elements continuously reappear. I'm just going to highlight a couple of examples. If we could go to photograph number 8, please. I believe it's page 8. Now, in this picture and in a number of the other pictures we see the remains of a person and that there's a card with numbers and letters printed on it. In this case, "NN 33." Could you describe what the information on that card is, if you can read it? Perhaps if we could zoom in on the card itself.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When exhumations were done, every body was brought out separately whenever possible and put in a body bag. The body bag was marked, first of all, with the date of the exhumation and the location so the exact site where the exhumation was performed, and this NN means unidentified person, and the cardinal number of the body beginning with 1. So all the information that was required in order not to mix up the bags and to make sure that each body bag contained a particular person was placed on the body bag, and after that the body bags were transported to a place where autopsies were done, and one and the same number followed the mortal remains from the beginning of that path to the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: I understand when you say the cardinal number 1, you're not referring to this specific photograph here but that it's the first body that was dug up would receive a number 1; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I just wanted to be more precise. Of course, it did not begin with number 33. It begins usually with number 1 and then we reached a number like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we turn to page 22. And could you describe what this photograph shows.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: When an identification is done, everybody is taken separately, and everything found on the body, on the arms, in the pockets, everything accompanying the body, all the objects are placed with the body, and during the post-mortem a description is provided not only of the body but also of all the accompanying objects such as clothing, jewellery, and especially documents that maybe relevant for identification. Because you have to know that before we had DNA, what was of particular interest to us and was key for the family to accept our identification were precisely these things such as keys or some personal item or a car key that could open a certain car ten years before. It was very valuable for the families to recognise the items that were found with the body, such as in this case, NN 33 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And in this case, how do we know for certain that these effects were found with this body, NN 30?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: At every exhumation special care was paid not to take some objects from the side and not put them in the wrong bag. So all the objects that were put in the body bag were found immediately on the body, around the neck, in the pocket, et cetera. Of course, in theory, you can argue there was a possibility that somebody confused these objects later, but we took strictly objects on the body itself, not around the body. Those items were included in the body bag, and they later were taken into account during identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, for the record, the identity of the body in -- shown in this particular picture and the personal effects can be established if you look at 65 ter documents 04043; 04046, page 9 in the English; and 05850, page 9 in the English. Could we go to page 69 of this booklet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And could you describe what this picture shows?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: You see on this photograph an open grave. What does that mean? When we started the exhumation, the principle we followed was not to touch the bodies or the objects on them until the entire grave is exhumed. We had to photograph the entirety, because only in that way, after a careful and professional exhumation, can bodies be retrieved one by one and placed in bags. We see a multitude of bones here. The bodies look very mixed up. But in view of the position of the bodies and in view of the fact that there was clothing on them, we could separate individual bodies with a high degree of accuracy. When the bodies are found exactly as they were at the time of death, we are able to separate them into individual bodies. However, in some situations, this may be impossible, such as in cases when bodies were damaged subsequently or thrown into wells, and then identification will not be possible in the same way. We will not be able to perform the exhumation so well or separate the bodies quite accurately.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could we have this photo booklet admitted. I just note that the other pictures are of a similar nature to this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit P361. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could we now get document 65 ter number 02472 on the monitor. And this is a report on exhumations in Eastern Slavonia, and it's written by John Clark.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Before we even see the document, do you know John Clark, and did you work with him at all?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know John Clark. He was in Zagreb several times, and we collaborated on autopsies on our premises when they -- or, rather, John Clark carried out identifications and processing of mortal remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And on page 1, near the bottom, under the heading "Receipt of the bodies in the mortuary," this is page 2 in the B/C/S, the report states: "At the completion of each exhumation, the bodies were transferred in sealed and labelled body bags to the mortuary in Zagreb." Did you see those bodies bags, and did you deal with those cases at all?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: When the bodies were delivered to Zagreb and we began with autopsies, just like in the Ovcara case, occasionally I would be present at autopsies together with my colleagues, and I saw those markings on the body bags.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: On page 2 of the English and B/C/S, this report sets out the methodology that they followed for autopsies in these cases, and you can see that in the indent the bullet points. Does that adhere to the usual professional standards for autopsies carried out?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I've seen this before. That is exactly the same way we do it. They went step-by-step. The bodies were received with their numbers. One by one they were placed on the tables, and then the autopsies were performed according to procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, if we could just turn over - and I'll get the page number now - to page number 12 in the English. And in the -- at the fourth bullet point this says that -- it's a summary of the findings, that the large majority of bodies found died from single gunshots to the head or neck. If we go back to the non-Ovcara table that you have already discussed earlier in your evidence and we look to the corresponding incident which is at paragraphs -- it's at pages 76 to 84 of the bigger of the two tables that was distributed to Your Honours and the Defence at the start of today's proceedings, and these are paragraphs 34 and 35 of the indictment, if you scan through those pages in your report from 76 to 84 looking at the cause of death findings, do they in general match the findings in the John Clark summary of findings? Again this is page 76 to 84. And while you're scrolling through those, I just note for Your Honours the easiest way I find to link the bodies referred to in exhumations such as this John Clark report to a specific paragraph of the indictment is to use the document that was admitted earlier today. It's 65 ter 05850, which lists the body numbers for the victims, and you can usually follow those numbers through to the other identification documents on the table to figure out which incidents from the indictment are at issue. So I will repeat my question. The summary of findings for the victims found at this Daljski Atar in John Clark's report is that the majority died of gunshot wounds to the head and neck. Does that match the findings in your table from reviewing the documentation?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I've just reviewed the table once again, and it is consistent with what you've just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 19 of the John Clark report which is on the monitor, and this is page 30 in the B/C/S. The second paragraph under the heading "Post-mortem findings." And it describes that two females and one male were located. In relation to the male, it states that the man had an obvious physical deformity and must have walked awkwardly and that this may have been related to a more generalised neurological condition. Firstly, is this deformity something that would be typically discovered by the forensic pathologist or an anthropologist or both?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: When mortal remains are examined, it is first done by a pathologists and then an anthropologist. In any case, damage like this, and it is relatively important damage, both the pathologist and anthropologist must have seen it, and that's why they wrote that this damage was important, must have made walking difficult, and that means that it was perfectly obvious to both specialists.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And how would this type of information assist to identify who the remains belonged to?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: For us any information of this type, something irregular, something unusual, something unhealthy such as this damage to the pelvis or the hip is very valuable, especially when we have a small group of missing persons. The smaller the group, information of this type is the more important. If we have a group of 1.000 people missing, there is a greater likelihood that two persons would have this type of deformity. However, the smaller the group, the more important this information is. It is very unlikely that two people in a small group or from a small village would have the same type of deformity. So this is one of the firmest evidence that we get for identification, changes on limbs, on bones that are evident and very helpful in identification, and it also means that the families would not have any problem with -- with the identification results.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: We would seek the admission of this report of John Clark, which is 02472.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit P362. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now could I get 05579 on the monitor, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And while that's coming up, this is a report on exhumations of wells, and it covers some of the same locations as the previous report that we saw. However, it goes into further detail on the personnel who were involved in these exhumations. On page 1, the first paragraph, the report notes that the Tribunal asked Colonel Ivan Grujic to exhume two of the alleged sites. Were you working with or for Colonel Ivan Grujic at this time? This is in the year 2000.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. We collaborated from -- was it 1994? Anyway, around that time he joined the commission for the detained and missing persons, and from that time we have been collaborating all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could I just ask that this not be publicly broadcast on the monitor because it's an internal document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: In terms of the exhumations that -- that are discussed here, are you aware of these exhumations from wells in Eastern Slavonia in -- near Borovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware. I know about these cases and I think most of them ended up in Zagreb. In any case, the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: On page 2 of the English and B/C/S it refers to some of the pathologists who were present. Do you recognise any of these people? Do you know them?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: On this list we see Dr. Dumancic, a forensic expert from Osijek who was in the field very often because he was based in Osijek which is very close to all those localities.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, if we could turn to page 8, and the corresponding pages are 9 through to 10 in the B/C/S. And here we have a description of the exhumation of a body marked with NN 35. Then if we continue to the top of page 9 in the English, we'll see that the report states -- it gives a possible cause of death. Do you see that in the first -- I'm not sure if you're looking at the English or the B/C/S, but it should be in English the first three lines at the top of page 9. Maybe if we could close-up on those.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, this body number relates to the very final victim listed in the large Ovcara table that has been provided, Marija Senasi. That is who we are discussing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Do you see what is listed for the possible cause of death?

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could we zoom in on the English to the first -- to the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see it. Thank you. Your question is what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Yes. What does the report state as to possible cause of death?

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: This should be page 9 in the English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This refers to a probable violent cause of death. This is the literal translation of what is written here. If you're asking me why that is written, I would have to read the report to see what the findings were.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And let's go to the corresponding report for this victim which is 65 ter 04185.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: If we could get that on the screen. And again that is listed on the non-Ovcara table, on the very final page. It is the autopsy report, the first document for Marija Senasi. If we could go to page 5 of the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, the cause of death --

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: This should be page 1 of the B/C/S translation. Is this 04185? I believe there is a translation issue. Some of these reports are written partly in English and partly in B/C/S, so the translation is a composite of the two. It should be in e-court the very -- the first document which is the original. If we could go to page 5 of that. And in the -- there should be a summary with the third paragraph. That's the document. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: So in the summary, in the third paragraph, the report states that the cause of death, it's possible this was gun-shot injury to the back of the neck, but it reaches the conclusion that the cause of death is unknown or unascertained. On what basis could they -- they make the suggestion that a possible cause would be gun-shot injury to the back of the neck?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: You're asking me something that is very hard to answer without the complete information. I can only speculate. I suppose that there is information to the effect as to what the expert found. He must have found something on the neck. Perhaps one part of the spine was missing, some part of the bone was missing. Things are not clear from the summary. I could be more precise if I had the full description of the findings of the skull, the cervical spine and so on and so forth. Then I would be able to answer your question. The way it is written in here does not tell us much about what happened. It says it is possible that the cause of death was a spinal -- or cervical spine wound, but I would have to see the whole -- the complete findings to see what the pathologist actually saw himself, and then I'd be able to answer your question properly. I apologise. The writing is again very small. There maybe a description here. Maybe if you blew up the summary, either in English or in Croatian, it doesn't really matter, maybe I would be able to answer your question actually. Yes, that's that. There is description which says that the -- there were parallel fractures in the body in the occipital part of the cranium which connected at the top. The description in itself doesn't say much, but further on it says that several cervical bones were missing. It says "neck bones," but there are no neck bones. There are cervical spine bones which are missing. And based on all the appearance where you can see that some of the cervical spine bones were missing and that there is a fracture of the skull, as a result of which the pathologist thought that the death may have been caused by the gun-shot wound of the neck. The finding was not specific, but it did say something. It did reveal a fracture. It did reveal some missing cervical spine bones. This is the upper part of the spine. And based on that, he provided the possibility which can be accepted as one of the possible explanations. We can still not be sure because we do not have a classical gun-shot wound or an entry-exit wound through either a skull or the cervical spine. That would be conclusive. But this is a nonspecific findings. There is a fracture, some cervical bones are missing. Something must have happened, but way don't know what. The event may be due to a gun-shot, so there may have been a gun-shot wound involved, but we cannot say that for -- for a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And could we have the report that we started on, which was 05579 admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would object to the admission of this document. It is internal report made by the investigator of the Prosecution, and it contained the information from the unknown witness, it is under page 1, that goes to the guilt of the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness has provided additional information about the people involved, such as Dumancic. He's provided additional explanation about the processes involved and confirmed that he's aware of these exhumations taking place. Now, I think the concerns of the Defence would go to the weight rather than the admissibility of this document, and you will hear more evidence in relation to the issues that my learned colleague has concerns about from a different witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Objection overruled. Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Last couple of questions, Dr. Strinovic. Looking at the overview, what is the approximate total number of missing persons from the conflict in Croatia -- I apologise. I should have waited for the Court Officer to have provided a number for that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Mr. Gillett.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And could it be admitted under seal, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It is only the internal memorandum you --

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Yes, it's 05579. Sorry, we shifted to a different document to help with the explanation of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And why should it be under seal?

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Because it's an internal document and it has the names of some of our investigators on it. I'm happy to look into the possibility of having that switched to a public document in due course, but currently in the interest of not frustrating the purpose of confidentiality, we'd prefer it to be admitted under seal at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And just to make sure that we come back to it, when would you be able to take a final position?

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Certainly by the end of tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. So it's admitted under seal for the moment, for the time being.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P363. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: I'll repeat my question. Going to the overview of your work in the conflict in Croatia, what is the approximate total number of missing persons from the conflict in Croatian in the 1990s?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Your question is impossible to answer, and I'll explain why. In 1991, when the commission was first set up at the end of 1991, the number of missing was very high. At one point a reference was made to 16.000 to 20.000 missing people, but they were not all dead. A certain number of them have been found. Some were in camps, prisons. Some had left the country, and so on and so forth. I can't tell you how many were reported as missing in 1991. The number was high. I can tell you what the situation is now, how many missing persons we have at the moment. First of all, those who were killed or went missing in 1991 and 1992, and then a large number who went missing in 1995. All of that in Croatia. I can tell you the figure as it stands now. I can't tell you how many went missing in 1991. It was a colourful number as it were, and it is very difficult to say how many really went missing as opposed to those who had gone missing and then were rediscovered or reappeared from somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: I'm looking for that approximate number for the current number of how many are missing.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: What I'm going to tell you is the information of the government's commission. From the 1st of January, 2013, Croatia is looking for 968 persons who have gone missing from 1991. Over 88 per cent of them are Croats, but there were others as well. So that's the data for the year 1991 and 1992. As for what happened in 1995, Croatia is still looking for 743 persons, residents of Croatia of Serb ethnicity, who went missing in 1995. Up to today, a total of 933 people have been exhumed, 572 were identified, which is a total of 61 per cent. At the moment, Croatia is looking for 968 people of -- plus those who went missing in 1995. We're talking about 743 people. So all in all, Croatia is still looking for nearly 1.700 missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And for the total number of people that died during the conflict, would that be greater than the 933 people that have been exhumed?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: I can only repeat what I have already said. 933 have been exhumed. 743 persons are still being searched, and those are the people that went missing in 1995. Did I make myself clear on that part?

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: That part is certainly clear, and it's okay if you don't have the information. I was just looking for a general figure of the number of people killed during the conflict in Croatia, but if that's not available, that's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: I understand the question. It's -- it's been put differently now. It's very difficult for me to tell you the exact number at the moment. I know that the figure was about 11.000-plus people, if that's what you're asking me. This is the figure that is referred to by the government, and that is the figure that should be correct. So this is the number of all those people who died, who were killed during the homeland war, 11.000-plus people.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Okay. Your Honours, that concludes my questions on direct exam. Do I understand that we're breaking at 2.15 or are we breaking at 2.00 today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Normally we break at 2.00, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: I wasn't sure because of the 15-minute delay at the start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But by all means, if this concludes your examination, I don't think we'll ask the Defence to start cross-examination for 15 minutes. I have one or two questions to ask, clarification questions. So you're done for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Yes, unless any questions arise if I can assist, but otherwise I'm done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You showed us and you tendered the list with the more or less 200 -- yes, about -- a number of about 200 victims of the Vukovar Hospital incident. Could we have some information about the origin of that document? It's the document with the 200 names of which 6 are -- were unidentified, and then 60 other names.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could I just say that's 65 ter 02498. I'm not sure what the exhibit number is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: 2498, sorry. 2498, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Is the question directed to myself or the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Whoever can answer the question. If the witness can answer the question, I would refer the witness to answer it. Mr. Strinovic, do you remember that list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, let's try and explain once again. When we're talking about the Vukovar Hospital, the list of the missing persons was compiled very early on, immediately after the event. There were several such lists. Some were expanded. However, the shortest list of the names contained over 290 names. That was the list of the missing persons. Second of all, when the persons who were found at Ovcara, the 200 bodies were identified, we ended up with 193 completed identifications. The names that you see from 1 to 200 or 1 to 193, those are the names of the peoples who were excavated from Ovcara, who were identified, and their body bags were marked by numbers from 1 to 200. And then on that list you have a large number of other names that are mentioned. Those are the people whose names were on the list of those who went missing from the hospital. They have never been found. They did go missing from the hospital. There are witnesses to that. But their bodies, the bodies of some 60 people who indeed did go missing from the hospital, their bodies were -- have not been found yet anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Strinovic, the purpose of my question was to know what this list is part of. I suppose it's not something on itself. Somebody compiled it. Where is it part of? What is it part of? Is it part of some kind of report? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: I could just offer that the information we have is that it's a fax -- it was attached to a fax received from the commission for detained and missing persons in March 2003, and I understand there's been various lists in relation to this matter sent back and forward at various times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Commission of which the witness was a member; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So do you -- do you recognise this list as a list made or compiled by the commission you were a member of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I recognise the list. I and my colleagues identified the victims. I recognise the names, the names of 193 people whose bodies have been identified over the past ten years or so, mostly by me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. And another little question about the booklet with photos that was shown to you. The inscriptions, the papers on the body bags, mention Lovas farm. Was that the location of the mass grave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was never there at Lovas farm, but I should have thought so, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We can perhaps pull up that document. It's 65 ter number 02444. Let's perhaps go to page -- page 10, in body bag with the number 20, and it says "Lakacija 4, Farma Lovas." Now, my question is: Is that Farma Lovas, is that part of the location where the body was found, or is it something else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, on several occasions, in one location such as Farma Lovas bodies were buried in several places. Farma Lovas is an area. It's a place. It's a location with several graves, and each of the graves was a location. Location 4 was where the body of an unknown person marked by number 32 was found at Lovas farm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I think your -- your question -- your answer is quite clear. I'll clarify my question to which I have an answer now. So Lovas farm on this paper does not refer to the place of death. It refers to the place of finding of the mortal remains. You agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So we take the break for today. You'll come back tomorrow morning at 9.00, and I must remind you that you are under oath, which implies that you are not allowed to discuss your testimony with anybody, and you are not allowed to speak to any of the parties at all. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do, Your Honours, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The usher -- the usher will escort you out of the court now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
